core: The working definition of a fixed cost, attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting, Volume 2: an unavoidable operating expense that does not change in total over the short term, even if the business experiences variation in its level of activity
The working definition of a variable cost, attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting, Volume 2: a cost that varies in direct proportion to the level of activity within the business

The per-unit flip — fixed cost per unit falls as volume rises while total fixed cost stays flat; variable cost per unit stays constant while total variable cost rises and falls — the key insight, taught with an original worked example
The relevant range as the bounded activity band within which the fixed/variable pattern holds — the honest caveat, with fixed costs stepping up outside the band

Why the split matters: pricing, break-even, and profit planning all start from the fixed/variable classification — the practical connection, with break-even-analysis referenced as a sibling topic only
Mixed costs named in one line — costs with both a fixed and a variable component — with cost-behavior referenced as a sibling topic only
The honest framing: the fixed/variable split is a decision tool, not a law — the reality check
supporting: Example fixed costs by business type: rent, insurance, managers'/administrative salaries, property taxes, equipment leases, straight-line depreciation (OpenStax Section 2.2)
The cost driver concept: any activity, such as units produced or labor hours, that causes a variable cost to rise or fall (OpenStax Section 2.2)
Total cost = total fixed costs + total variable costs (OpenStax Section 2.2)
Example variable costs: direct materials (e.g., wood, beans, sand), direct labor hours, fuel (CFI; OpenStax Section 2.2)
Classification as the basis for managerial decisions and cost control, e.g., trading high variable labor for stable fixed machinery costs at sufficient volume (CFI; OpenStax Section 2.2)
outOfScope: Cost behavior depth — step costs, committed vs discretionary fixed costs, high-low method, and separating mixed costs (sibling topic: accounting:foundations:cost-behavior; referenced only)
Break-even calculations and the break-even formula (sibling topic: accounting:foundations:break-even-analysis; referenced only)
Contribution margin, margin of safety, and operating leverage (break-even-analysis and cost-behavior siblings)
Managerial accounting as a whole (sibling topic: accounting:foundations:managerial-accounting; referenced only)
Budgeting mechanics (sibling topic: accounting:foundations:budgeting; referenced only)
Cost-volume-profit analysis in general, job order costing, process costing, and activity-based costing — named only where a source does so, not taught

claims.claim: A fixed cost is an unavoidable operating expense that does not change in total over the short term, even if a business experiences variation in its level of activity — the working definition attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting, Volume 2.

A variable cost is one that varies in direct proportion to the level of activity within the business — the working definition attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting, Volume 2; CFI states the same pattern (costs that fluctuate with the volume of production).
Fixed costs remain fixed in total but change on a per-unit basis: as the level of activity rises, the per-unit fixed cost falls.
Variable costs remain the same per unit but change in total: total variable costs rise and fall as the level of activity rises and falls.
Total cost is the sum of total fixed costs and total variable costs.
A cost driver is any activity that causes the organization to incur a variable cost; examples include direct labor hours, machine hours, units produced, and units sold.

The relevant range is a specific activity level bounded by a minimum and a maximum amount; within it, managers can predict revenue or cost levels, and outside it, fixed costs step up to higher amounts (e.g., a second machine or overtime).
Mixed costs have both a fixed and a variable component (e.g., a fee paid per month plus an amount per unit of activity).

Classifying costs as fixed or variable is what lets managers control costs and use cost data to make decisions and plan for the future — pricing, production, and investment choices all lean on the classification.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is a fixed cost fixed forever?
positions: A fixed cost never changes, so a lease signed today behaves identically at any volume and any time.
Fixed costs are fixed only in total, over the short term, and within the relevant range; leases end, capacity is added, and fixed costs step up beyond the band.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: OpenStax defines fixed costs with both qualifiers — 'in total' and 'over the short term' — and introduces the relevant range as the band within which predictions hold, with step-ups beyond it. The lesson teaches the definition with those qualifiers and closes with the honest framing that the split is a tool, not a law.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is a given cost — say, labor — fixed or variable?
positions: Labor is a variable cost because workers are paid for the hours they work.
Labor is a fixed cost because staff get steady salaries.
It depends on the arrangement: hourly production labor varies with output while salaried staff do not.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both OpenStax (variable costs include labor applied directly to production; fixed costs include managers' and administrative salaries) and CFI (direct labor hours as variable) support the arrangement-dependent view. The lesson classifies by how a cost actually responds to activity and includes the labor case as a common mistake.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's boilerplate claims ('Fixed And Variable Costs is a foundational concept in Accounting', 'College courses use fixed and variable costs as a building block for later discussions, assignments, and decisions') carried no sources and no substance; they were replaced entirely.

The draft's quickCheck questions ('Which approach best shows understanding...?', 'Why is context important...?') were generic study-skills items with 3 options, not accounting questions; all five questions were rewritten from the verified content.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the unsourced draft with a sourced lesson: working definitions now attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting, Volume 2 (Section 2.2), corroborated by CFI.

Added the per-unit flip as the central insight with an original worked example (Roast & Ember: $2,400 fixed total ÷ 800 = $3.00 per pound vs ÷ 1,600 = $1.50 per pound; beans constant at $1.50 per pound). All arithmetic verified: 2400/800 = 3.00, 2400/1600 = 1.50, 800 × 1.50 = 1200, 1600 × 1.50 = 2400.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Accounting, Volume 2: Managerial Accounting, Section 2.2: Identify and Apply Basic Cost Behavior Patterns
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21 (openstax.org served the full section to curl this session) and cross-checked against an Internet Archive capture of the same page. Supports: the working definition of a fixed cost as an unavoidable operating expense that does not change in total over the short term even with variation in activity; fixed costs staying fixed in total but changing per unit, with the per-unit fixed cost falling as activity rises (screen-printing example: $1,000 monthly rent); the working definition of a variable cost as varying in direct proportion to the level of activity; variable costs staying the same per unit while changing in total (ink per T-shirt); the cost driver definition (any activity that causes the organization to incur a variable cost; examples direct labor hours, machine hours, units produced, units sold); total cost as the sum of total fixed and total variable costs; mixed costs having both a fixed and a variable component (hotel occupancy tax example); the relevant range as a specific activity level bounded by a minimum and maximum within which managers can predict revenue or cost levels, with step costs (quality-inspector example) stepping up beyond the band; and classifying costs to control costs, make decisions, and plan for the future (Boeing feature). Page footer bars LLM ingestion; used REFERENCE_ONLY, facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Fixed and Variable Costs
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B (reputable secondary). Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports: fixed costs do not change with increases or decreases in units of production volume while variable costs fluctuate with volume; example fixed costs (rent, advertising, insurance, depreciation) and variable costs (direct materials such as wood, direct labor hours); the steering-wheel illustration — $250 variable cost per unit with total variable cost scaling (1, 500, 1,000, 1,500 units) while total fixed cost ($550,000 factory rent) stays constant; classification as important for assembling product-cost schedules, for capital decisions (trading high variable labor for stable fixed machinery costs, with volume and volatility as trade-offs), and as ingredients in costing methods (job order, process, activity-based). Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
